explanation: 'Specialise' is followed by the preposition 'in', not 'at' — 'The company specialises in designing...'.
After the modal 'will' the base form of the verb is required, so 'will replaced' must be 'will replace'.
A planned future trip takes 'will visit', not the modal 'should visit', which wrongly expresses obligation/advice.
Physical distance/position needs 'farther' (or better, 'next to'); 'further' denotes additional degree, not literal distance.
The future perfect is 'will have graduated'; 'will had graduated' is an incorrect verb form.
'Principals' (heads of institutions) should be 'principles', meaning moral rules or beliefs.
The team received the action, so the passive 'were still overwhelmed' is required instead of the active perfect 'had still overwhelmed'.
The other verbs ('had', 'talked') are past, so the present 'go' must be 'went' for tense consistency.
'Nevertheless' is a conjunctive adverb and cannot join the clauses here; a contrast conjunction like 'but' or 'whereas' is needed.
'Fastly' is not a word; 'fast' serves as both adjective and adverb, so it should be 'ran fast'.
'Ouch!' expresses sudden pain and does not suit a dry, refusing tone; an interjection like 'Well!' or 'Alas!' would fit.
'Every' is always followed by a singular noun, so it must be 'Every student in the hostel'.
The restaurant has already been specified, so the definite article is required: 'the interior of the restaurant'.
After the linking verb 'became' an adjective is needed, so 'violently' must be 'violent'.
The correct order places the ordinal-type word first: 'the next few days', not 'the few next days'.
Latin comparatives ending in '-ior' such as 'superior' take 'to', so it should be 'superior to him'.
'Information' is an uncountable noun and has no plural form, so 'no informations' should be 'no information'.
The action verb 'performed' needs the adverb 'well', not the adjective 'good' — 'performed extremely well'.
The noun meaning 'result' is 'effect'; 'affect' is a verb, so it should be 'no effect'.
'Brought about' means 'caused'; for publishing a book the correct phrasal verb is 'brought out'.
The idiom is 'in store for', so 'what fate had it store for them' must be 'what fate had in store for them'.
The correct idiom is 'forget all about it', not 'forget all on it'.
The participial phrase 'After seeing that...' and the past-tense main clause are both correct, so there is no error.
'Indifference' is a singular uncountable noun, so the verb must be 'was well noticed', not 'were'.
The present perfect passive needs the third form of the verb: 'he has been warned', not 'warn'.
Cupholders are set into a surface, so the preposition should be 'in the cupboards', not 'on the cupboards'.
'Accuse' takes the preposition 'of': 'accused of stealing', not 'accused for stealing'.
The fixed expression is 'at the dinner table' (or 'at table'), not 'on the dinner table'.
'No other option but to work hard' is the correct idiomatic structure, so the sentence has no error.
The phrase needs 'of Germany'; 'off' means away from and is wrong here.
With a possessive time expression like 'last week's', no article is used: 'for last week's Sunday Supplement'.
'Was gazing longingly at the toy' correctly uses the adverb with the verb 'gaze' and the preposition 'at', so there is no error.
The required word is 'off side/offside'; 'of side' is not a valid form.
The idiom is 'take criticism to heart', not 'in heart'.
'Confide' takes 'in' when trusting a person: 'King Lear confided in his daughter'.
After 'while', the verb takes the -ing form: 'careful while executing the orders'.
'Aim high' uses the flat adverb 'high'; 'highly' means 'very much' and is wrong here.
'Decide' takes 'on' when choosing something: 'deciding on a gift for them'.
Past participles used with verbs of feeling take 'much/greatly', not 'very': 'are much admired'.
The intensifier needed is 'quite' (fairly/completely); 'quiet' means silent.
'The famous author and actor' has a single article, showing one person holding both roles, so the verb must be singular: 'is being honoured'.
The relative clause 'Those who are late' already supplies the subject, so the extra pronoun 'they' is superfluous; it should be 'will not be allowed'.
'Information' is an uncountable noun taking a singular verb, so 'were given' must be 'was given'.
The fixed collocation is 'afraid of', not 'afraid from', so it should read 'afraid of darkness'.
'Everyone' is singular and 'except' is a preposition, so the correct form is 'except her has travelled'.
'Marry' takes a direct object without a preposition, so it should be 'He married a rich heiress'.
'Quiet' (silent) is confused with 'quite' (fairly/completely); the sentence needs 'quite unpleasant experiences'.
'Appears to have got its name from' is a correct perfect infinitive structure with proper prepositions, so the sentence is error-free.
'On behalf of' means 'representing someone', which is illogical here; the idiomatic phrase should be 'for the sake of awareness' or 'to spread awareness'.
The introductory 'It' is singular, so the verb must be 'It has been only'.
'Put' is an irregular verb whose past form is also 'put', so 'putted' is incorrect.
A plural noun, not a possessive, is needed as the object of 'requested', so it should be 'the teachers'.
A modal must be followed by the base form of the verb, so 'Would you liked' should be 'Would you like'.
'Cheap' begins with a consonant sound, so the article must be 'a cheap dumping ground'.
'Pleased' takes the preposition 'with', so it should be 'were pleased with John's domain knowledge'.
An adverb is needed to modify the action verb 'marched', so 'fearless' must become 'fearlessly'.
'Effort' here is uncountable, so the quantifier must be 'much effort at all', not 'many effort'.
An infinitive takes the base form of the verb, so 'wanted to known' should be 'wanted to know'.
In a third conditional with inverted 'Had you...', the main clause requires 'would have', so 'we will have' is wrong.
'Help someone with something' is the correct collocation, so 'along this heavy box' should be 'with this heavy box'.

The sentence is grammatically sound: 'allege that there is a delay in procuring stationery due to the faulty purchase orders' uses correct tense, gerund after the preposition 'in', and an acceptable causal phrase.
The main clause verb 'behaved' is past, so the time clause needs the past form 'came', not the present 'come'.
'Expensive' begins with a vowel sound, so the article must be 'an expensive car'.
A specific fact requires the definite article: 'After knowing the truth'.
'Hardly' is already negative, so 'nothing' creates a double negative; it should be 'We hardly knew anything'.
'was always been' mixes past simple with a past participle; the correct form is 'He had always been a grumpy man'.
'Opposition' here denotes a particular political group, so it takes the definite article: 'with the opposition'.
The singular subject 'My younger brother' needs a singular verb, so 'were attending' should be 'is attending' (with 'these days').
'Neetu' is a singular proper noun subject, so the verb must be 'has been', not 'have been'.
'Oculist' starts with a vowel sound, so the article must be 'an oculist'.
After the auxiliary 'had', the past participle is required: 'had passed away'.
'Honest' begins with a vowel sound (the 'h' is silent), so it takes 'an honest'.
The adjective 'cold' must be modified by an adverb, so it should be 'get extremely cold'.
'The same' cannot replace a plural noun object here; it should be 'I dry them'.
Names of sacred books and epics take the definite article, so it must be 'the Mahabharata'.
In sentences beginning with 'Here', the verb agrees with the real subject 'the bus', so 'comes' is required.
'Hurry' begins with a consonant sound, so the article must be 'a hurry'.
'More good' is an incorrect double comparative; it should be 'as his health is not good' or 'is no better'.
The main clause is in the past ('I started'), so the time clause needs 'After I retired'.
A degree is received 'from' an institution, not 'into' it.
Clock times with parts of the day take 'in': 'at five in the morning', not 'on the morning'.
'has being' is not a valid verb form; the present perfect requires 'has been' — 'The audience has been angry'.
The verb 'enter' is transitive and takes no preposition, so 'entered the house' is correct, not 'enter into the house'.
The action verb 'describes' must be modified by the adverb 'vividly', not the adjective 'vivid'.
Things lying under the ground are 'beneath/under the surface'; 'in the surface' is the wrong preposition.
The man performed the action, so the active 'who committed the theft' is required, not the passive 'was committed'.
The fixed collocation is 'invisible to the naked eye', not 'invisible from'.
The adverb 'skilfully' is needed to modify the action 'handle', not the adjective 'skillful'.
'Belong' is a stative verb of possession and has no continuous form: 'these days belongs to my brother'.
'Looked' here is a linking verb, so it takes the adjective 'decent', not the adverb 'decently'.
'Both ... and' joins two subjects to form a plural subject, so the verb must be 'have won'.
'Hurry' is itself a verb, so the modal takes the bare infinitive: 'You must hurry' (or 'must be in a hurry').
'Straightly' is not a valid form; the adverb of 'straight' is 'straight', giving 'quickly and straight'.
A period of time with the perfect tense takes 'for', so it should be 'for three years', not 'by three years'.
An enclosed space takes 'in': 'no tables in the classroom', not 'at the classroom'.
After the preposition 'of' a gerund is required: 'knowledge of working with junior colleagues'.
The idiom is 'spending beyond one's means', so 'against' is the wrong preposition.
'Accuse' is followed by 'of', not 'for': 'accuses him of a lack of morality'.
'Tell' takes an object plus the infinitive: 'told Rahul to wait', so 'on' is incorrect.
The teaching began before the 2019 visit, so the earlier action needs the past perfect continuous: 'had already been teaching'.
'One of the major challenges' is the singular subject, so the verb must be 'was', not 'were'.
'Children' is a plural subject, so the verb should be 'listen', not 'listens'.
'The number of + plural noun' always takes a singular verb, so 'are constantly decreasing' should be 'is constantly decreasing'.
The plural subject 'The students' needs the plural verb 'ask', not 'asks'.
The hint word 'usually' signals present indefinite tense, so 'hasn't take' must be 'doesn't take'.
The correct phrasal verb is 'held up' (delayed); 'held upon' is not an idiomatic combination.
The past continuous passive is 'was being operated'; 'was been operated' is an incorrect passive form.
'Unless' already carries a negative sense, so adding 'doesn't' makes it a double negative; it should be 'unless one goes'.
With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the nurse', so it should be 'was present'.
The singular subject 'it' requires 'doesn't matter', not 'don't matter'.
The verb 'stand' (tolerate) is followed by a gerund, so it should be 'his father beating him'.
The fixed collocation is 'rich in' when denoting abundance of a substance, so 'is rich with' should be 'is rich in'.
During an earthquake one takes cover 'under' a table, not 'above' it; the preposition is wrong.
'As well as' does not change the number of the subject, so the verb must agree with 'The boy': 'was' instead of 'were'.
The past-tense clause 'did not see' requires the earlier verb in the past too: 'There were some monkeys'.
The parallel past narration needs 'got on the train to Mumbai'; 'get' and 'by' are both wrong here.
The reason after 'get upset' takes 'at' (or 'about'), so 'for scoring less' should be 'at scoring less'.
The past-tense context ('pulled in') requires 'it took Joseph some time', not the present 'take'.
A comparative degree is intensified by 'much' or 'far', not 'very'; it should be 'much richer than Jim'.
With 'go to a place', the relative construction must be 'to which he went', not 'for which he went'.
'Lived close to the train station' and the contrast marker 'yet travelled by bus' are both idiomatic and grammatically correct, so the sentence has no error.
Possession by a person is shown with a possessive adjective, so 'the tight coat of him' must be 'his tight coat'.
When pronouns of all three persons are joined in a positive statement, the order is 2-3-1: 'You, she and I'.
The main clause of a future time clause needs a finite verb: 'it will be much quicker', not the bare 'it be'.
A modal like 'should' is always followed by the base form, so 'should sorted out' must be 'should sort out'.
The subject is the singular 'The strain'; the words after 'caused by' do not change the number, so the verb should be 'was more than'.
Of two past actions, the earlier one takes the past perfect, so 'has done everything' must be 'had done everything'.
'Start' is followed by a gerund or infinitive, so 'has started bring' should be 'has started bringing' (or 'to bring').
The relative pronoun's verb agrees with its antecedent 'a thing', which is singular, so it should be 'thing that is not easily'.
'Fail' is intransitive here and takes no passive form; the correct phrasing is 'he had failed to arrange the money'.
'No sooner' is always correlated with 'than', not 'that': 'No sooner had Kavya started ... than the web connection was lost'.
'The reason ... was because' is redundant; the correct construction is 'The reason ... was that'.
The singular subject 'This renowned university' needs the singular verb 'provides'.
'Each one of the children' is a singular subject, so the verb must be 'requires individual attention'.
'Beside' means 'by the side of', while 'besides' means 'in addition to'; here it should be 'beside her mother'.
In compound nouns of the type noun+preposition+noun, the first word is pluralised: 'His sons-in-law'.
The adjective 'different' takes the preposition 'from', so it should be 'different from what he had expected'.
'Persist' is followed by 'in' + gerund, so 'persists to ask' must be 'persists in asking'.
'Scarcely/Hardly had ...' is completed by 'when', not 'then': 'when the doorbell rang'.
'My friend and Principal of this college' describes one person, Mr. Das, so the verb must be singular: 'has retired'.
'Effort' is countable here, so 'Much efforts' is wrong; it should be 'Many efforts' (or 'Much effort').
'Evidence' is an uncountable noun and has no plural form, so 'sufficient evidences' should be 'sufficient evidence'.
After 'It is essential that', the subjunctive (base form) is required: 'every applicant submit', not 'submits'.
Parallelism with the nouns 'prudence, propriety' requires the noun 'avoidance of early disclosure', not the gerund phrase 'avoiding of'.
'Every employee' is singular, so the pronoun must be singular: 'regardless of his or her designation', not 'their'.
'Each of + plural noun' takes a singular verb, so 'have submitted' should be 'has submitted'.
'Handwriting' is uncountable and used in a general sense, so no article is used: 'in legible handwriting'.
The singular countable noun 'collection' needs an indefinite article: 'an extensive collection of journals'.
'Superior' is already comparative in sense, so 'more superior' is a double comparative; use 'was superior to'.
'Information' is uncountable and has no plural, so 'useful informations' should be 'useful information'.
'Advice' is uncountable; 'practical advices' should be 'practical advice'.
'Consist' is always followed by 'of', so it should be 'consists of specialists'.
After 'insisted that', the structure is 'should + V1' or the subjunctive base form: 'every employee should submit / submit the form', not 'must submits'.
The main subject is the uncountable noun 'evidence', so the verb must be singular: 'has been deemed'.
'No sooner' at the start of a sentence requires inversion: 'No sooner was the verdict delivered than...'.
With the negative inversion 'Little did', the base form of the verb follows: 'Little did the board know'.
'Information' is uncountable, so it must be 'Much information was shared', not 'Many informations were shared'.
The possessive determiner is 'Its'; 'It's' means 'it is', which does not fit before 'strategic location'.
After the inversion 'Rarely does he', the main verb stays in the base form: 'Rarely does he go'.
C introduces the participants and the play, D identifies it as a tribute to Karnad, B explains the division into 10-minute segments, and A follows up on 'those allotted minutes', giving CDBA.
In the cleft structure 'It was at ... that ...', the connector must be 'that', not 'where'; so '(2) where the bilateral accord was formally endorsed' is wrong.
The subject 'The committee's recommendation' is singular, and the intervening phrase 'notwithstanding its ambiguity' does not change it, so 'were considered' must be 'was considered'.
The omission happened before the past-tense realisation, so the past perfect 'had omitted' is required instead of 'has omitted'.
With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the HR officer', which is singular, so 'were informed' should be 'was informed'.
The plural subject 'recommendations' needs 'have been considered', not 'has been considered'.
'Not only ... but also' must join parallel elements; since 'not only' is followed by the object 'the board members', 'but also to the investors' wrongly adds 'to'.
The comparison is illogical: the delay was never avoided, so 'much sooner than it actually was' is faulty; the unreal conditional needs simply 'the delay could have been avoided'.
The head subject is the singular noun 'The belief', so the verb must be 'has caused', not 'have caused'.
The two modifiers of 'appeal' should be joined by 'or' ('so lacking in substance, or so plainly designed'); 'nor' is incorrect as no second negative clause follows.
With 'not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the second subject 'the members', so 'has been charged' must be 'have been charged'.
'Fail' is followed by an infinitive, so 'had failed recognising' should be 'had failed to recognise'.
With the cleft 'It was not until ... that', no inversion is used and the verb must be finite: 'that the corporation initiated', not 'did the corporation initiated'.
'Feedback' is an uncountable noun and cannot take the article 'a'; it should be 'detailed feedback'.
The adjective meaning 'main' is 'principal'; 'principle' is a noun, so 'principle issue' should be 'principal issue'.
The fixed expression is 'owing to', not 'owing of'.
'All that is required' is a singular subject phrase, so the verb should be 'is a two-thirds vote', matching the singular 'is required'.
'Advice' is uncountable and has no plural form, so 'their individual advices' should be 'their individual advice' (or 'pieces of advice').
'Hardly' is correlated with 'when', not 'than', so '(2)' should read 'when dissenting opinions were voiced'.
'No sooner' is followed by 'than', not 'when', so '(2)' should begin 'than the opposition'.
In 'there' sentences the verb agrees with the following singular noun 'a time', so it should be 'has there been a time'.
Adjectives ending in '-ior' like 'superior' are followed by 'to', never 'than'; correct form is 'is superior to'.
'will been working' is an incomplete verb form; the future perfect continuous requires 'will have been working'.
The past continuous 'was walking' fixes the sentence in the past, so the verbs must be 'called me and asked'.
'Interior' refers to physical inside space; for a country's own affairs the correct adjective is 'internal problems'.
'back in' is the wrong phrasal verb here; the police would tell agitators 'to back off/back out'.
'gave up' means to surrender or quit; distributing prizes requires 'gave away' (or simply 'gave').
The compound subject 'He and his friends' is plural, so the auxiliary must be 'do not', not 'does not'.
The verb 'banged' needs an adverb, so 'violent' must become 'violently'.
A comparison between two things with 'than' takes the comparative degree: 'is better than', not the superlative 'best'.
The singular proper-noun subject 'Mr. Surya' needs 'has', and the correct word is 'ulterior motive', not 'interior'.
The 'so...as' structure takes the positive degree, so it should be 'so good as', not the comparative 'better'.
A profession mentioned generally takes the indefinite article: 'to become an engineer', not 'the engineer'.
Numbers like hundred take 'a' in such expressions: 'a hundred reasons', not 'the hundred reasons'.
The sentence is about legal permission, not physical ability, so 'able to drink' must be 'allowed to drink'.
After 'have' the third form of the verb is required: 'I have sung', not 'I have sing'.
'Talk' collocates with 'to' when addressing someone, so 'talks to anybody' is correct.
The time range needs the preposition 'till/to', so 'still 10 p.m.' should be 'till 10 p.m.'.
A clause subject needs the nominative pronoun and a time conjunction: 'when she was 23', not 'as her was 23'.
The 'as...as' construction takes the positive degree, so it must be 'as smart as', not 'as smarter as'.
'for more than a decade' signals present perfect and the verb must agree with 'he', so 'who has worked' is correct.
The head of the subject is the singular noun 'The fact', so the verb must be 'highlights', not 'highlight'; the intervening 'that'-clause does not change the number.
'Capable' is followed by 'of' + gerund, so it should be 'capable of addressing', not 'capable for addressing'.
'Not only ... but also' must join parallel structures; 'designed to modernise' requires 'but also to improve transparency', not 'improving'.
'Chance' takes either 'to' + base verb or 'of' + gerund, so 'to scrutinising' should be 'to scrutinise' (or 'of scrutinising').
'Not only' is followed by a noun phrase ('institutional failure'), so 'but also' must also take a noun phrase (e.g., 'but also the growing assertiveness of civil society'), not a 'that'-clause.

The participle 'Having completed' needs an agent as subject, but the passive clause makes 'the revised proposal' the subject, creating a dangling modifier; it should be 'the committee then forwarded the revised proposal'.
'Whether' must be balanced by 'or whether' (or a bare 'or'), not 'or if'; also the indicative 'was' is required rather than 'were'.
'Underlie' is an irregular verb whose past form is 'underlay' (past participle 'underlain'), so 'underlied' is wrong.
After 'recommended that', the subjunctive base form is required: 'that the proposal be reconsidered', not 'is reconsidered'.
The subject 'Much of what seems to be coordination' is singular, so the verb must be 'is', not 'are'.
Parallelism requires 'partly to pressure ... and partly to legal uncertainty'; 'partly because of' breaks the structure after 'was linked to'.
'Capable' is never followed by an infinitive; the correct form is 'capable of resolving'.
The modal perfect is 'might have prevented'; the extra 'had' in 'might have had prevented' is ungrammatical.
The singular subject 'no official clarification' requires the singular verb 'was circulated'; the prepositional phrase does not affect agreement.
After 'seeks to', the correlative must join parallel base verbs: 'to neither prosecute ... nor overlook'; the second 'to' destroys the parallelism.
The relative clause 'who had been predicting' is misplaced far from its antecedent 'the investors'; it should immediately follow that noun.
'Together with' is an additive connective that does not change the number of the subject, so the singular 'The managing director' requires 'was'.
A 'that'-clause used as subject is singular, so the verb must be 'was surprising', not 'were surprising'.
The noun 'need' takes the preposition 'for' when followed by a thing required: 'an urgent need for robust ethical frameworks'.
'Necessitate that' triggers the subjunctive, so it must be 'every regional office conduct', not 'conducts'.
The pronoun 'I' takes 'am', not 'are'; the correct form is 'I am dancing'.
'Very' cannot modify a comparative, and the verb 'barks' needs an adverb: 'very loudly' (or 'much louder').
'Luggage' is an uncountable noun and has no plural form, so it should be 'my luggage'.

With the third-person singular subject 'It' in the simple present, the verb must be 'rains'.
The past participle 'injured' must be modified by the adverb 'badly', not the adjective 'bad'.
The correlative 'not only' must be completed by 'but also', so segment 2 should read 'but also the rigidity'.
The subject is the singular 'The assumption', so the verb should be 'has led', not 'have led'.
'not ... but' must join parallel structures; the noun phrase in (1) is paired with a 'that' clause, so (2) should read 'but its assumption, without empirical evidence, of'.
The correlative is 'not only ... but also' placed before parallel verbs: 'not only indicates ... but also weakens', not 'does not only indicate'.
The main verb 'triggered' is past, so the reporting verb must also be past: 'who stated they'.
After the modal 'will', the bare infinitive is required: 'comply', not 'complies'.
'Which' refers to the plural 'warnings' in a past context, so it should be 'had been ignored', not 'has been ignored'.
A 'what' clause as subject takes a singular verb, so it should be 'was not the scheme's objectives'.
The subject is the singular 'The report's focus', so the verb must be 'ignores'.
With 'neither ... nor' joining two singular subjects, the verb agrees with the nearer singular noun: 'seems'.
The subject is the singular 'The claim', so the verb should be 'indicates'.
'Every one of + plural noun' is singular, so it should be 'was instructed'.
A completed past failure needs the simple past 'failed', not the past continuous 'were failing'.
The comparison must be between like items: 'more reliable than that of anyone else' (or 'than anyone else's').
After 'are made to', the base form of the verb is required, and it must be parallel with 'protect', so 'safeguarding' should be 'safeguard'.
'Yet' is not used in affirmative statements of this type; the correct adverb is 'still' — 'We still have time'.
'All' requires a plural noun, so the irregular plural 'mice' must replace 'mouse'.
'Made of' is used when the original material is still visible in the product; 'made from' implies the material has been transformed, so it should be 'made of silver'.
The correct phrasal verb for exhausting a supply is 'run out of', not 'run down of'.
'No one' is not followed by 'of'; with a plural group the correct pronoun is 'None of them'.
With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'I', so 'are interested' should be 'am interested'.
After the auxiliary 'did', the base form of the verb is required — 'Did you tell him'.
A numeral adjective used before a noun stays singular and hyphenated — 'an eight-year-old girl'.
An embedded (indirect) question keeps normal word order, so 'how can we' should be 'how we can'.
'It's' is the contraction of 'it is'; the possessive determiner 'its' is needed — 'since its formation'.
'Beside' means 'next to', while 'besides' means 'in addition to', so it should be 'The girl beside you'.
In indirect speech the interrogative inversion is dropped, so 'where had I' should be 'where I had'.
The fixed idiom is 'get away with', not 'get away among' — so it should be 'with lying'.
'Plan' is followed by an infinitive, not 'for' + gerund — 'planning to settle'.
The clause states a point of time, so the time conjunction 'when' is needed instead of 'as'.
The head subject is the singular 'venue' ('for the wedding' is only a modifier), so the verb must be 'has not yet been finalised'.
The adjective 'ready' is followed by an infinitive, so it should be 'ready to leave'.
A clause introduced by 'when' does not take a future tense; it should be 'when the bell rings'.
'Whole' preceding a singular noun requires the definite article — 'The whole country'.
The correct idiom is 'take (someone) to task', meaning to reprimand; 'at task' is wrong.
The idiomatic expression is 'went for a ride'; 'afar' is not used with 'ride'.
'More harder' is a double comparative; the correct form is 'The harder you work'.
'Before' here is a preposition, so it must be followed by a gerund: 'Before taking this medicine'.
A relative clause describing a 'place' needs 'where', not 'when': 'a place where two or more rivers meet'.
'Such' must be completed by 'that' (such a long speech that everybody felt bored), so 'such' is wrongly used with 'but'.
For more than two persons the reciprocal pronoun is 'one another', and 'each another' is never correct.
'A large number of' is followed by a plural countable noun: 'of workers'.
'Time' here is uncountable, so it takes 'much', not 'many': 'much time'.

The subject 'A large amount of money' is singular, so the verb must be 'was wasted'.
